speaker: NORA
text: Think about the last time you walked through an automatic door at a hospital. Or drove into an underground car park under a rising gate. Or noticed a heavy fire door in an office corridor, the kind that's meant to close on its own if there's a fire. You probably didn't give any of them a second thought.

speaker: JAMES
text: And that's exactly the point. They're supposed to just work. But every one of those doors and gates is a machine, with motors, sensors, springs, closers and control units. Many of them are safety equipment. A fire door that doesn't close, or a smoke vent in the roof that doesn't open, can turn a small fire into a disaster. So in many countries, including Germany, they have to be inspected and maintained regularly, by qualified people.

speaker: NORA
text: Those people are technicians, and there aren't enough of them. Today's company is a German group that has been buying up the small, family-run firms that employ them, at a remarkable pace. Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills, with a European team as well. Today it's ENTRO, a Hamburg-based group of technical service companies for doors, gates, fire safety and access systems.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: the group's own news releases, mostly in German, the private equity firm's announcement, advisers' case studies and trade press in Germany and the UK. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a figure comes from the company, we'll flag it. And nothing here is legal, safety or investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And one quick clarification. There's an unrelated American cybersecurity company with a similar name, which was acquired by another firm in 2026. That's not our ENTRO. Ours is about doors and fire safety.

speaker: NORA
text: Good to clear that up. So, the one-sentence version.

speaker: JAMES
text: ENTRO buys regional service firms that inspect, repair and install entrance systems like doors and gates, fire-safety systems like smoke and heat extraction and fire doors, and access and security systems, for business and public-sector customers, mainly in Germany and now also in the UK and the Netherlands.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting?

speaker: JAMES
text: Speed. The group was founded in 2022. By its own figures it went from nine companies in September 2025 to sixteen by August 2026, with about five hundred staff, twenty-five sites and around eighty million euros of revenue. That's a huge amount of change in a short time. And in a business like this, AI comes after something much more basic: getting sixteen companies onto common systems.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. Where is it based?

speaker: JAMES
text: The private equity firm and the group's website give Hamburg as headquarters. Some of the group's earlier releases give Munich as the company's legal seat and the place it was founded. So, founded in Munich in 2022, run from Hamburg today, is the simplest way to put it. We didn't open the official registry entry to confirm.

speaker: NORA
text: Who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: The chief executive is Sonja Foremny. The chief operating officer is Jan Ingo Buschmeyer. The founders, Claudio Tubach and Philipp Westphal, are managing directors. Nikolas Diedrich is also listed in group leadership. And in September 2026, Marc Groenewegen was named chief executive of the group's Dutch partner companies.

speaker: NORA
text: And the size? You mentioned numbers that moved quickly.

speaker: JAMES
text: They really did, and I want to give each figure with its date, because they come from different releases. In January 2025, the group said it had about thirty million euros of revenue and about two hundred staff. In September 2025, when the private equity deal was announced, about fifty million euros, two hundred and fifty staff, of whom one hundred and seventy were technicians, sixteen locations, nine companies and more than four thousand five hundred customers.

speaker: NORA
text: And then?

speaker: JAMES
text: In February 2026, an adviser's case study said more than three hundred and fifty staff across Europe. In June 2026, twelve holdings, more than four hundred staff and twenty-two sites. And in August 2026, sixteen companies, more than five hundred staff and twenty-five sites across Germany, the Netherlands and the UK, with about eighty million euros of revenue.

speaker: NORA
text: So revenue nearly tripled in about eighteen months.

speaker: JAMES
text: On the group's own figures, from about thirty to about eighty million euros between January 2025 and August 2026. Almost all of that is from acquisitions, in our inference, though organic growth is in there somewhere.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a number that tells you about the quality of the revenue?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, and it's a good one. In January 2025 the group said about eighty percent of its revenue came from existing customers. That's a company figure, and it's from before the recent deals. But it tells you the business is built on recurring relationships: inspection and maintenance contracts that renew, rather than one-off installations.

speaker: NORA
text: And revenue per person?

speaker: JAMES
text: If you divide eighty million euros by five hundred staff, you get roughly one hundred and sixty thousand euros per head. That's our arithmetic, not a reported figure. It's typical of a labour-heavy technical services business. Growth depends on technicians.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the history. Founded only in 2022?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. It's a young platform. The idea, from what the group says, was to build a partnership-style group of regional service firms, many of them family-owned, often facing a succession problem: the owner wants to retire and there's no obvious successor.

speaker: NORA
text: And who backed it at the start?

speaker: JAMES
text: A firm called NGC Nachfolgekapital is named as a co-founding party. The word "Nachfolge" means succession in German, so the name itself tells you the investment idea: succession capital for family businesses. We didn't find details of its stake today.

speaker: NORA
text: And then Levine Leichtman came in.

speaker: JAMES
text: On the seventeenth of September 2025, the private equity firm announced a majority investment in ENTRO, from its second European fund, in partnership with the founders and management. Terms weren't disclosed. So, as we record, it's held the business for a little over a year.

speaker: NORA
text: Very early in the hold.

speaker: JAMES
text: Very early. And what's happened since is the classic buy-and-build acceleration that a new private equity owner often brings: more capital, more deal capacity, a push into new countries.

speaker: NORA
text: What did the group say it would do with the investment?

speaker: JAMES
text: The September 2025 release, in German, listed among its plans to develop its digital solutions further. That's a general statement, not a specific programme, but it's worth noting. And back in January 2025, the group had already named two main challenges: the shortage of skilled workers and digitalisation.

speaker: NORA
text: So the company itself recognises the digital gap.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does, which is a good starting point. Naming the problem is the first step.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the customer's problem. Who are the customers, and what do they need?

speaker: JAMES
text: The customers are businesses and public bodies with buildings. Industrial sites, warehouses and logistics centres, hospitals and care homes, offices, retail, schools, public buildings. Anyone with doors, gates, fire-safety systems and access control that have to work and, in many cases, have to be inspected by law.

speaker: NORA
text: Explain the inspection part.

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, in Germany and across much of Europe, many powered doors and gates, fire doors and smoke and heat extraction systems must be inspected at regular intervals, often annually, by qualified people. The rules come from a mix of building regulations, workplace safety rules and technical standards. The details vary by type of equipment and by German state, and I won't pretend to know every rule. The point is that building owners carry legal responsibility, and they need a documented inspection to show they've met it.

speaker: NORA
text: And smoke and heat extraction is what?

speaker: JAMES
text: Systems that open vents, usually in the roof or high on walls, to let smoke and heat escape in a fire. That keeps escape routes clearer and helps firefighters. In German it's abbreviated R W A. If those vents don't open when needed, the consequences can be very serious. So they're inspected and maintained regularly.

speaker: NORA
text: So what does the customer buy?

speaker: JAMES
text: Usually a recurring inspection and maintenance contract, plus repairs when something breaks, plus occasionally new installations or upgrades. And here's the important bit. A large site might have dozens or hundreds of doors and gates from many different manufacturers, installed over decades. The customer wants one firm that can service all of them.

speaker: NORA
text: Rather than calling each manufacturer.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. That's ENTRO's pitch: service that's independent of any single manufacturer, often shortened to O E M independent, for original equipment manufacturer. One provider, many brands. At the same time, some of its companies are also authorised partners of particular manufacturers, which gives them access to parts and training. For example, Lütjen, which joined in 2026, is an authorised partner of Hörmann, Novoferm and Teckentrup, three well-known German door and gate makers.

speaker: NORA
text: What's driving demand?

speaker: JAMES
text: According to the group and the private equity firm: stricter regulation, rising awareness of security, energy efficiency, which matters because badly sealing doors and gates waste heat, the skilled-labour shortage, which pushes customers to outsource, and owners of small service firms looking for succession. That last one drives the supply of companies to buy, rather than customer demand.

speaker: NORA
text: Why does energy efficiency come into a door business?

speaker: JAMES
text: Think of a large logistics hall in winter. Its loading doors open and close hundreds of times a day. If they're slow, badly sealed or left open because a sensor's faulty, a lot of heated air escapes. Fast, well-maintained doors and good seals can cut that loss. As general background, with energy prices a big concern in Germany in recent years, building operators pay more attention to that than they used to. So maintenance and upgrades become partly an energy decision.

speaker: NORA
text: And security awareness?

speaker: JAMES
text: Access control and intrusion systems, who can get in where, and what happens if someone tries to force a door. Businesses and public bodies have become more conscious of that, according to the group. And it links naturally to doors and gates, because the door is where access control physically happens.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about how the group is put together. Is it one company or sixteen?

speaker: JAMES
text: Both, in a way. ENTRO buys regional firms and, crucially, the firms usually keep their local names. M and S Türen und Tore in Bisingen, Lütjen in Worpswede near Bremen, SWI Württemberg in Pfullingen, and so on. Other names in the group include KHT, Gebrüder Kuttner, Torpado, Wassermann, ITS, TSB and an electrical firm called Elektro Ingenieur Dietmar Wolf, plus the Dutch companies. And a parts business called OK Parts, in Düren.

speaker: NORA
text: Why keep the local names?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because in local services, the name is the relationship. A facilities manager at a hospital in Swabia has been calling the same local firm for twenty years. They know the technicians. If that firm suddenly becomes an anonymous national brand, the customer may wonder whether the service will change. Keeping the name reassures customers and staff. It's common in buy-and-build strategies of this kind.

speaker: NORA
text: And what does the group add?

speaker: JAMES
text: In its January 2025 release, the group named shared purchasing, IT and recruiting as synergies. So the idea is that local firms keep their identity and customer relationships, while the group provides scale benefits behind the scenes: better parts prices, shared systems, help with hiring, and a succession solution for owners.

speaker: NORA
text: And it's meant to be a partnership.

speaker: JAMES
text: The group calls its approach partnership-based. Owners and managers often stay on, sometimes with a stake. That's similar to what we've seen in other episodes in this series: the founder doesn't just sell and leave.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's imagine it from the seller's side. What does an owner get from joining? Invented, of course.

speaker: JAMES
text: Picture Herr Bauer, sixty-four, who built a door and gate service firm with twenty technicians over thirty years. His children have other careers. His best technician is good with machines but doesn't want to run a business. Without a successor, his options are to sell to a competitor, to a manufacturer, or slowly wind down. Joining a group like ENTRO lets him sell, often keep some role for a transition period, keep the company's name and keep his team employed.

speaker: NORA
text: And what does he worry about?

speaker: JAMES
text: Whether his customers will be looked after, whether his staff will be treated well, and whether head office will make everything bureaucratic. Those are the questions any group like this has to answer convincingly, because word travels among owners in a region. If one owner has a bad experience, the next three may say no.

speaker: NORA
text: So reputation among sellers is an asset too.

speaker: JAMES
text: In buy-and-build, it's a crucial one. The group's ability to keep buying depends on being a home owners want to sell to.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned OK Parts. Why does a parts company matter?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view it's quietly strategic. If you service doors and gates from many manufacturers, getting the right part quickly is a big deal. A technician who arrives without the right motor or sensor has to come back another day. A group-owned parts business can stock and buy parts across brands for all sixteen companies. That's a scale advantage local firms don't have.

speaker: NORA
text: And the service lines?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three, as the group describes them. Entrance systems: doors, gates, barriers, loading bays. Fire safety: smoke and heat extraction, fire doors, escape route systems. And access and security: access control and intrusion systems. Bundling those three for one customer is part of the pitch.

speaker: NORA
text: And the meetings you mentioned?

speaker: JAMES
text: The group's news headlines show a managing directors' meeting in Hamburg in September 2026, where it reported continued growth, and a service managers' meeting in Dortmund in October 2026. We only saw the headlines. But bringing the managers of sixteen companies together regularly is how a group like this starts to build a common culture and common ways of working.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go through the recent deals.

speaker: JAMES
text: In February 2026 ENTRO entered the UK with two deals. First, Bi-Fold Rolfe, an industrial door specialist, announced on the eighteenth of February. Sources disagree slightly on its location: an adviser's case study says Southampton, while another source describes it as serving the South and Central UK. Then Aberdeen Alarm Company, a fire and security firm in Aberdeen, Scotland, reported on the twenty-seventh of February.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the UK business?

speaker: JAMES
text: From the February 2026 coverage, about one hundred staff, five locations and about ten million euros of revenue. An accounting firm, Saffery, which advised on the UK entry, described it as a UK platform built from two deals.

speaker: NORA
text: And in Germany?

speaker: JAMES
text: On the tenth of June 2026, Lütjen in Worpswede, a door, gate and fire-protection specialist in northern Germany, which took the group to twelve holdings. Trade press dated that one the eighteenth. Then on the fifth of August 2026, SWI Württemberg in Pfullingen, in the southwest, with twenty-five staff. With that, the group said it had sixteen companies, twenty-five sites and about eighty million euros of revenue, and it said it planned growth in the Rhein-Neckar and Rhein-Main regions, around cities like Mannheim and Frankfurt.

speaker: NORA
text: And the Netherlands?

speaker: JAMES
text: The group has Dutch partner companies, and in September 2026 named Marc Groenewegen as their chief executive. We didn't find the dates or names of the Dutch deals. Several of the German deals are also undated in what we found.

speaker: NORA
text: So that's about four dated acquisitions in six months.

speaker: JAMES
text: About four in roughly six months, February to August 2026, plus others we can't date. In my view, that's a fast pace for a company that, in September 2025, had nine firms.

speaker: NORA
text: What's the logic of the UK and Netherlands moves?

speaker: JAMES
text: Our inference: the same model works in any country with lots of small, family-owned service firms, inspection-heavy regulation and a skills shortage. The UK and the Netherlands fit. But each new country adds a new language or legal system, new standards and new customers. The UK platform is still small, so it'll need more deals to reach scale.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the market?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a reliable figure for the German market, and I'm not going to estimate one. What we can say is that it's fragmented, with many regional independents, which is what makes the roll-up possible.

speaker: NORA
text: And who are the competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: Several kinds. First, large security services groups. Securitas Deutschland, the German arm of the Swedish group Securitas, which has more than ninety German sites and offers fire alarms, access control and intrusion systems, but within a broader security services model that includes guarding.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Manufacturers with their own service arms. dormakaba, the access and entrance systems group, which sells door hardware, entrance systems and service. ASSA ABLOY, a global access group with about sixty-four thousand staff, where entrance automation is one of several areas. GEZE, a family-run company from Leonberg, founded in 1863, with more than three thousand staff, making door and window automation and offering its own service. And Hörmann, which describes itself as Europe's leading supplier of doors and gates, with service through dealer and branch networks.

speaker: NORA
text: And Hörmann's network is the one Lütjen sits in.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. It's an interesting dynamic. Some of ENTRO's companies are authorised partners of the very manufacturers that also offer service. So the manufacturers are suppliers, partners and competitors at the same time.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fire and security integrators, like Chubb Fire and Security in the UK. And there's an interesting name echo: an Italian access-control group, CAME, bought a UK company called ENTROTEC. Despite the name, that's not ENTRO. And then there are the many regional independents, which are both competitors and potential acquisitions.

speaker: NORA
text: How does ENTRO compete against the big manufacturers?

speaker: JAMES
text: Independence and locality. A manufacturer's service team naturally prefers its own products. A building with ten different brands of doors wants someone who'll service all of them. And a local firm with technicians twenty minutes away can respond faster than a distant national team. In my view, that's a real advantage, as long as ENTRO's companies can get the parts and technical information for many brands.

speaker: NORA
text: Is the UK market much different?

speaker: JAMES
text: In broad strokes, as general background, the UK has its own regulations and standards for fire doors, fire alarms and powered doors and gates, and its own trade bodies and certification schemes. So the technical knowledge transfers, but the paperwork, the rules and the customer expectations differ. And the UK market has its own larger players, like Chubb, alongside lots of independents, which is presumably what makes it attractive for ENTRO's model.

speaker: NORA
text: And is anyone using AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: We found no AI-native challenger in this market. But there's a very interesting signal from September 2026. A German trade publication reported on a feasibility study by a smoke and heat extraction firm called RWA-BADEN and a company called KItelligence, funded by the state of Baden-Württemberg. It found that AI knowledge assistants built over maintenance data reduced the time technicians spent searching for information, and it recommended a pilot. No market numbers. And to be clear, that's a sector signal, not ENTRO.

speaker: NORA
text: But it points in an interesting direction.

speaker: JAMES
text: It points exactly where I'd point ENTRO, as we'll get to.

speaker: NORA
text: So, where is ENTRO on AI?

speaker: NORA
text: What systems do the sixteen companies use?
chapter: AI and digital at ENTRO today

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't know, and this is the key inference. When you buy sixteen family-run firms, you usually inherit sixteen ways of working. Some might use a field-service management package. Some might use a simple scheduling tool and paper inspection forms. Some might rely on an office manager's spreadsheet and an experienced dispatcher's memory. And each will have its own customer records, its own inspection report formats and its own parts lists. That's typical in roll-ups, and nothing ENTRO has published suggests otherwise.
chapter: AI and digital at ENTRO today

speaker: NORA
text: What does a good field-service platform actually do?
chapter: AI and digital at ENTRO today

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, it holds every customer, every site and every asset, like each door, gate or smoke vent, with its make, model, installation date and history. It schedules inspections automatically based on due dates. It dispatches technicians to jobs, ideally with their skills and location in mind. It gives technicians a mobile app for inspection checklists, photos and signatures. It tracks parts used, triggers invoices and quotes, and reports on performance. Many vendors sell such systems.
chapter: AI and digital at ENTRO today

speaker: NORA
text: So it's the operating system of the business.
chapter: AI and digital at ENTRO today

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a good way to put it. And the asset history is the part that makes AI possible later. If every fault on every door model across sixteen companies is recorded consistently, you have the training material for a diagnostic assistant.
chapter: AI and digital at ENTRO today

speaker: NORA
text: So the foundation for AI isn't there yet.
chapter: AI and digital at ENTRO today

speaker: JAMES
text: Publicly, no. And that's not a failing. It's simply where a fast-growing, one-year-old platform would be. The point is the order of operations. You can't build a useful AI assistant over sixteen separate data silos in different formats and two or three languages. First you need a common field-service platform. Then AI.

speaker: NORA
text: You've said that before in this series.
chapter: AI and digital at ENTRO today

speaker: JAMES
text: I have, and I'll keep saying it. For roll-ups, the first AI project is usually a data and systems project.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make it concrete. Walk me through a day for a technician. Invented, not real.

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's call him Jonas. He works for one of ENTRO's regional companies in southern Germany. He's been fixing doors and gates for fifteen years. He's in a van by seven. Today: three inspections, a breakdown call and a new customer.

speaker: NORA
text: First stop?

speaker: JAMES
text: A logistics warehouse with twelve high-speed roll-up doors and four fire doors. Annual inspection. He tests each door: safety edges, light barriers, emergency stop, spring tension, drive. He checks that the fire doors close and latch properly. He fills in an inspection report for each, maybe on a tablet, maybe on paper. One door has a worn safety edge. He notes it and recommends a repair.

speaker: NORA
text: And then?

speaker: JAMES
text: At ten, a call comes in from the office. A care home's automatic entrance door is stuck open. That's a security and heating problem, and for a care home, residents with dementia might wander out. Jonas is the closest technician. He drives over. It's a brand he's seen only twice before. The control unit shows a fault code he doesn't recognise.

speaker: NORA
text: What does he do?

speaker: JAMES
text: Today? He calls a colleague who might know. The colleague's on a roof. He searches on his phone for the manual. He finds a PDF in another language. He tries a couple of things. Forty-five minutes later he works out it's a sensor fault, but he doesn't have the part in the van. He sets the door to a safe manual mode and books a return visit.

speaker: NORA
text: So the care home waits.

speaker: JAMES
text: And Jonas loses half a day on the return trip. Then in the afternoon, another inspection, at a school, of smoke and heat extraction vents. He checks the vents open, the control panel, the batteries, the triggers. Again, a report. Then a quote visit at a new customer's industrial site, where the facilities manager wants one firm to take over all their doors and gates from three previous suppliers.

speaker: NORA
text: And at the end of the day?

speaker: JAMES
text: Paperwork. Inspection reports to finish, the parts order for the care home, a note for the office about the worn safety edge at the warehouse so someone can send a quote. Maybe an hour of admin after a full day of physical work.

speaker: NORA
text: Where do the problems lie?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three places. Finding information: the fault code at the care home. Having the right part: the return trip. And paperwork: the evening reports. Each is a waste of a scarce technician's time.

speaker: NORA
text: Now replay it with a common platform and an AI assistant.

speaker: JAMES
text: Jonas arrives at the care home. On his tablet, the system already knows this customer and this door, because every asset is in one database. He types or says the fault code. The assistant, built on the manufacturer manuals and the group's own fault histories from all sixteen companies, replies: this code on this model usually means a failed motion sensor; here's the test to confirm; here's the part number. And it adds that technicians at two other group companies fixed the same fault last year.

speaker: NORA
text: So he's drawing on the whole group's experience.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. That's the power of putting sixteen companies on one platform. Then the system checks stock: OK Parts has the sensor, and a colleague's van ten kilometres away has one too. The dispatcher arranges a hand-over. Jonas fixes the door in one visit.

speaker: NORA
text: And the inspection reports?

speaker: JAMES
text: He records readings as he goes, and the system drafts the reports and flags the worn safety edge as a repair opportunity, which automatically creates a quote for the office to review. By the time he's back in the van, the paperwork is mostly done. He reviews and signs.

speaker: NORA
text: What doesn't change?

speaker: JAMES
text: The physical work, his judgement, and his responsibility. The assistant suggests. Jonas decides. If he disagrees with the suggested diagnosis, he goes with his own experience. And the inspection is still his signed record.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk challenges.

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, integration. Sixteen companies across three countries in about a year. Each with its own systems, culture and customer relationships. Getting them onto common systems without losing customers or staff is the biggest operational challenge.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: The skilled-labour shortage. The group itself names it. Technicians are the constraint. Every hour lost to searching, return trips and paperwork is an hour not spent on billable service. And new technicians take time to learn the variety of equipment out there.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's stay on that for a moment. How does the shortage play out in practice?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, Germany has a well-known shortage of skilled tradespeople. Many experienced technicians are approaching retirement, and fewer young people are entering the trades. For a firm like Jonas's, that means it may turn down work, or take longer to respond. It also means the knowledge in experienced technicians' heads, which brand does what, which fault code means what, is at risk of walking out of the door when they retire.

speaker: NORA
text: So knowledge capture is part of the problem.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a big part, in my view. An AI assistant built on fault histories is, in a sense, a way of preserving and sharing that knowledge. And there's a recruiting angle. Young technicians expect digital tools. A firm that still runs on paper forms is less attractive to them.

speaker: NORA
text: Third challenge?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, the digital starting point. No public digital product, portal or software. No named technology leader. That's a lot to build.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Inconsistent group disclosures. Nine, twelve, sixteen companies; two hundred to five hundred staff; sixteen to twenty-five locations. Some of that is real growth. Some may be counting differences. Internally, our inference is that consolidated reporting across sixteen companies is still developing, which matters for running the business and for a future buyer.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fifth, the sub-scale UK platform. About a hundred staff and ten million euros. It needs more deals to be efficient, and running a second country with different standards adds complexity.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me push back on integration. If local firms keep their names and relationships, why force common systems on them?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fair question. I wouldn't force everything. Keep the names, the local managers, the customer relationships. But some things should be common: one field-service system for scheduling, asset records and inspection reports; one parts and purchasing process through OK Parts; one finance and reporting system. Without those, you can't share knowledge, you can't dispatch across company boundaries, and you can't use AI across the group. And you can't show a buyer one set of numbers.

speaker: NORA
text: How do you get local owners to agree?

speaker: JAMES
text: Show them what they get: faster parts, fewer return trips, less evening paperwork, help with recruiting. And involve their best technicians and dispatchers in choosing the platform. People resist systems that are imposed and adopt systems they helped shape.

speaker: NORA
text: Opportunities.

speaker: JAMES
text: The highest-value one, in my view, is an AI field-service assistant: a shared knowledge base over manuals, fault histories and inspection reports, plus AI-assisted dispatch. The payoff is in technician hours and how quickly new technicians become productive.

speaker: NORA
text: Can you size it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Only as an illustration, built on assumptions, not facts. Take the one hundred and seventy technicians from the September 2025 figure. If each saved twenty minutes a day, that's roughly fourteen thousand hours a year, or about nine full-time technicians' worth of time at sixteen hundred productive hours each. In a market where you can't hire enough technicians, freeing nine technicians' worth of capacity is significant. And the group has grown since, so the number could be larger.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: The common field-service and customer relationship platform across all sixteen companies, before the next wave of deals. Every deal added before the platform exists makes the integration bigger. Shared purchasing, IT and recruiting were already named as synergies, so this fits the group's own plan.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Parts and purchasing. Use OK Parts as the group-wide parts business across manufacturer brands. Better prices, better availability and fewer return trips.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cross-selling and recurring contracts. Bundle door, fire safety and access service into one multi-year maintenance contract for existing customers. A warehouse that uses one ENTRO company for doors might also need its smoke vents and access control serviced. One contract, one invoice, one inspection calendar.

speaker: NORA
text: Fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Regional expansion. Rhein-Neckar and Rhein-Main, as the group has said. Building out the Netherlands under its new chief executive. And growing the UK platform. Each new region ideally lands on the common platform from day one.

speaker: NORA
text: And pricing? You raised the hourly risk earlier.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. If maintenance contracts are priced per inspection or per asset, efficiency becomes margin. If repairs are billed by technician hour, faster diagnosis means less revenue per job, but also more jobs per day and happier customers. In a labour-short market, my view is that ENTRO will usually have more work than technicians, so efficiency translates into growth. Over time, moving more customers to fixed-price service agreements that cover inspection, preventive maintenance and a response-time promise would make that link explicit.

speaker: NORA
text: And acquisitions generally?

speaker: JAMES
text: Succession deals. The group markets itself to owners looking for a successor, which, given the age profile of many family business owners, as general background, is a steady source of targets. The more attractive ENTRO is as a home, with good tools and a good culture, the more owners will want to join.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a customer-facing digital opportunity too?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, our inference. A customer portal where a facilities manager can see every door, gate and fire-safety system across their sites, with inspection status, upcoming due dates and open repairs. Larger customers increasingly expect that kind of visibility. It makes the service stickier and helps with cross-selling. But again, it depends on having one asset database first.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's look at it from the customer's side for a moment. Another invented example.

speaker: JAMES
text: Say a hospital group in the Rhein-Main area, with four hospitals, has around six hundred doors, gates, fire doors and smoke vents between them. Today its facilities manager, call her Frau Keller, deals with three or four different service firms, each with its own inspection schedule, report format and invoices. Before an inspection by the fire authorities, she spends days pulling together certificates from different folders and emails.

speaker: NORA
text: And what would she want instead?

speaker: JAMES
text: One contract covering doors, fire safety and access across all four sites. One portal showing every asset, its last inspection, the next due date and any open defects. Reports in one format. And a guaranteed response time for breakdowns, especially for entrances to emergency departments. If ENTRO can offer that, through its local companies and a common platform, it wins the whole contract rather than a slice.

speaker: NORA
text: And AI helps how?

speaker: JAMES
text: In small but meaningful ways. Drafting inspection reports consistently. Summarising open defects across sites for her monthly meeting, ranked by safety risk. Predicting which doors are likely to need major repairs next year, so she can budget. None of it replaces the technician, but all of it makes Frau Keller's job easier, which is what makes her renew.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI bet?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: The AI technician assistant and dispatch tool, built on one field-service platform. But I'd be explicit that in the first hundred days, most of the work is the platform, not the AI.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: So how would you run it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: map what exists. Which systems each of the sixteen companies uses, how they record assets and inspections, where manuals and fault records live. Pick a target field-service platform, ideally with input from dispatchers and senior technicians. Choose two or three pilot companies, ideally one that already has decent digital records and one that doesn't, plus one of the recent German acquisitions.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: What's the hardest part of that mapping, do you think?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Data quality and language, in my guess. Older firms may have asset records that are incomplete, or no asset records at all, just customer names and addresses with notes. Fault histories may be in free-text notes in German, Dutch or English, written in each technician's shorthand. Inspection report formats will differ. So before any AI, someone has to decide what a standard asset record looks like and clean the data into that shape. It's not glamorous. It's essential.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Start migrating the pilot companies' asset and customer data to the common platform. At the same time, start building the knowledge base: collect manufacturer manuals, the pilot companies' fault histories and inspection reports, and sit down with a few senior technicians about the faults they see most. Clean it, tag it by brand and model. That's the raw material for the assistant.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And sixty to a hundred?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Put a first version of the assistant in the hands of ten or fifteen technicians in the pilot companies. Measure the basics: time to diagnose, first-visit fix rate, return trips, time spent on reports. Ask the technicians what helps and what's annoying. And measure dispatch: travel time, response time to breakdowns.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: And then?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: If the pilots show fewer return trips and faster diagnoses, use that as the business case for rolling the platform out to all sixteen companies, with the assistant as the reason technicians want it. And publish the results inside the group, at the next service managers' meeting.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Any governance questions?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: A few. Manufacturer manuals may have copyright and licensing terms, so check what can be loaded into a knowledge base. Customer data, including site layouts and security system details, is sensitive, especially for access and intrusion systems, so security controls matter. And the assistant must never replace the technician's judgement on safety equipment. Its suggestions are advice. The inspection result is a human decision.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: Who owns it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: JAMES
text: Someone has to. If there's no technology leader today, hiring one, or appointing one from inside with real authority, is step zero. And pair that person with the chief operating officer, because this is as much an operations project as a technology one.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first hundred days

speaker: NORA
text: What can other businesses learn from ENTRO?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four lessons. First, in a roll-up, the first AI project is a systems project. Every company in this series that's grown by acquisition faces this. The sooner you build the common platform, the cheaper it is.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, capture knowledge before it retires. Many trades businesses depend on experienced people's memories. An AI assistant built on fault histories and manuals turns individual memory into group knowledge. That's valuable whether or not you call it AI.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, in a labour-constrained business, AI is about capacity, not cuts. ENTRO can't hire enough technicians. Anything that frees technician time is growth. That's also the honest and motivating message for staff.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, keep local identity but share the back end. Customers and technicians value the local name. Scale comes from parts, systems and knowledge shared behind the scenes. ENTRO's model already does the first part. The second is the opportunity.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a lesson about naming your problems?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, and it's a small one I liked. ENTRO publicly named digitalisation and the skills shortage as its challenges in January 2025. Many companies wouldn't. Naming them creates accountability, and it tells potential sellers and recruits that leadership sees the same problems they do.

speaker: NORA
text: And a fifth, maybe on speed?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Speed of acquisition and speed of integration need to stay in balance. If you buy faster than you integrate, the integration backlog grows with every deal. At some point it's worth slowing deals briefly to build the platform, so that every future deal lands on it.

speaker: NORA
text: Risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, manufacturer disruption. If manufacturers move service toward remote monitoring and direct contracts, connected doors and gates that report their own faults, the independent service model could narrow. That's our inference. Two, AI affecting the revenue model. If AI cuts technician hours per inspection, and contracts are priced by the hour, revenue per contract falls unless pricing moves to fixed fees. Also our inference.

speaker: NORA
text: Three?

speaker: JAMES
text: The labour shortage itself, which limits growth no matter what. Four, integration risk across sixteen companies in three countries. And five, larger rivals like Securitas, dormakaba and ASSA ABLOY bundling service with their products.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me push on the first. Couldn't connected doors be an opportunity for ENTRO too?

speaker: JAMES
text: Absolutely, and I'd argue it should be. If doors and gates increasingly report their own status, then a multi-brand service provider that can read data from many manufacturers' systems and act on it is very valuable. That would need partnerships with manufacturers and a strong digital platform. Which, again, comes back to building the foundation first.

speaker: NORA
text: And from the owner's point of view, what's the timeline?

speaker: JAMES
text: The investment is about a year old, so a sale is not on the near horizon, as far as we know. But a future buyer of a sixteen-plus company group will ask how integrated it really is. One platform, one set of numbers, measurable improvements in technician productivity, and a credible digital story would all support a higher valuation. In that sense, the platform and the AI aren't just operating projects. They're part of the equity story.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four things. First, any announcement of a common field-service platform or a technology leader. Second, the next deals, especially in Rhein-Neckar, Rhein-Main, the Netherlands and the UK. Third, any digital product for customers, like a portal. And fourth, any AI pilot, perhaps similar to the feasibility study we mentioned from Baden-Württemberg.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: What does ENTRO do?

speaker: JAMES
text: Keeps doors, gates and fire-safety systems working and inspected, across many brands.

speaker: NORA
text: Most impressive number?

speaker: JAMES
text: From nine companies to sixteen in under a year.

speaker: NORA
text: Most important number?

speaker: JAMES
text: About eighty percent of revenue from existing customers, by the group's early-2025 figure.

speaker: NORA
text: AI today?

speaker: JAMES
text: None visible.

speaker: NORA
text: First step?

speaker: JAMES
text: One field-service platform across all sixteen companies.

speaker: NORA
text: Best AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: A technician assistant built on manuals and fault histories.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a trades business should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Ask your three most experienced technicians to list the faults they fix most often, and write down how. That's your first knowledge base.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Optimist. Sticky revenue, real demand and a clear path. But the path starts with plumbing, not AI.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. ENTRO is a young German group, founded in 2022 and run from Hamburg, that buys regional service firms for doors, gates, fire safety and access systems, keeping their local names while sharing purchasing, IT and recruiting. Levine Leichtman took a majority stake in September 2025, and since then the group has grown, by its own figures, from nine companies to sixteen, with about five hundred staff, twenty-five sites and around eighty million euros of revenue, entering the UK and the Netherlands along the way. It has no visible AI, and it has named skilled labour and digitalisation as its main challenges. In our view, the first job is a common field-service platform, and the best AI bet on top is an assistant that helps technicians diagnose faults and finish their paperwork.

speaker: JAMES
text: And my closing thought. In a business where the scarcest thing is a skilled technician's time, the best AI is the one that turns one technician's experience into everyone's. But you can only do that once everyone is on the same system.
